cards.front: Can someone watching the network see which site you visit over HTTPS?
cards.back: Yes, usually: the domain name leaks via DNS and the TLS handshake; the path, headers and body are encrypted.Visible to the network?Server IP addressyesDomain nameusually yesURL path and queryno, encryptedHeaders and bodyno, encrypted

cards.front: A service listens on `127.0.0.1:8000` and another on `0.0.0.0:8000`. Who can connect to each?
cards.back: `127.0.0.1`: only programs on the same machine. `0.0.0.0`: anyone who can reach any of the machine's interfaces.127.0.0.1:80000.0.0.0:8000Listens onloopback onlyall IPv4 interfacesSame machineyesyesOther machinesnoyes, if firewall allows

cards.front: An app in a Docker container listens on `127.0.0.1:8000`. Why does `-p 8000:8000` still not reach it?
cards.back: The container's `127.0.0.1` is its own loopback. Forwarded traffic arrives on another interface, so the app must bind `0.0.0.0`.

cards.front: Why do most DNS lookups use UDP instead of TCP?
cards.back: The question and answer each fit in one packet, so skipping TCP's handshake makes the lookup faster.

cards.front: Your program makes one TCP send of 10 KB. Will the receiver always get it in one read?
cards.back: No, TCP is a byte stream without message boundaries, so the data may arrive split across several reads.

cards.front: Find the processes using port 5432
cards.back: `sudo lsof -i :5432`

cards.front: List the open TCP connections on this machine
cards.back: `ss -t`

cards.front: Does the browser padlock mean a website is trustworthy?
cards.back: No, only that the connection is encrypted to whoever controls that domain; scam sites get certificates too.

cards.front: List the listening TCP services, showing which address and port each one is bound to
cards.back: `ss -tlnp`

cards.front: Show which program owns each listening TCP port
cards.back: `sudo ss -tlnp`

cards.front: Make curl skip certificate checks on https://example.com (for testing only)
cards.back: `curl -k https://example.com`

cards.front: Does traffic sent to `127.0.0.1` go out through the network card?
cards.back: No. It goes through the loopback interface `lo`, which the kernel handles without the traffic ever leaving the machine.

cards.front: Why does a fresh PostgreSQL install refuse connections from other machines?
cards.back: `listen_addresses` defaults to `localhost`, so PostgreSQL listens only on the loopback interface.

cards.front: List the TCP ports waiting for incoming connections
cards.back: `ss -tl`

cards.front: How does `curl` decide whether to trust example.com's certificate?
cards.back: It follows the chain of signatures up to a root certificate already in the machine's trust store.example.com certificateintermediate CAsigned byroot CA (trust store)signed by

cards.front: What does a TLS certificate tie together?
cards.back: A domain name and a public key, signed by a certificate authority that vouches for them.

cards.front: What does TCP do before any data is sent?
cards.back: A three-way handshake: the client sends SYN, the server replies SYN-ACK, the client answers ACK.clientserver1. SYN3. ACK2. SYN-ACK

cards.front: If a UDP packet is lost on the way, who resends it?
cards.back: Nobody, unless the application itself notices and sends it again; UDP never retries.

cards.front: List listening TCP ports as numbers, not service names
cards.back: `ss -tln`

cards.front: How does TCP make sure data that got lost still arrives?
cards.back: The receiver acknowledges what it got; if the sender gets no acknowledgement in time, it resends the data.
